title: Abbott directs TCEQ to halt all data center permits pending ERCOT and water audits
whatHappened: On September 21, 2026, Gov. Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits sought by data center projects until the ERCOT audit is complete. He also said no state agency should advance data center regulatory approvals until that audit information is in hand. TCEQ must report on compliance to the Governor's Office by October 19, 2026. A TCEQ spokesperson described the pause as covering air and water permits and authorizations for infrastructure directly supporting data centers. Abbott also said he will ask the Legislature next session to eliminate financial incentives for data centers.
whyItMatters: With the grid-interconnection freeze already in place, this halts the state environmental permits needed for on-site and off-grid generation. In practice it is the closest thing to a statewide pause in the second-largest U.S. data center market. Even behind-the-meter projects that bypass ERCOT now face a state permitting gate.
affected: Texas data center developers, including behind-the-meter and island-mode gas generation projects (e.g., West Texas and Permian campuses); hyperscalers; gas turbine and generator suppliers; TCEQ permit applicants.
watchNext: TCEQ compliance update to the Governor due October 19, 2026. ERCOT/PUCT audit report targeted for about December 10, 2026. The 90th Legislature convenes January 2027, where incentive repeal and statutory limits are expected.

The directive names no specific permit types, and its legal basis for binding an independent agency has not been tested.

title: Abbott orders audit of ERCOT data center queue; ERCOT pauses Batch Zero interconnection study
authority: Governor Greg Abbott (letter to PUCT and ERCOT); ERCOT; PUCT
whatHappened: On August 3, 2026, Gov. Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to conduct a 'comprehensive verification and audit' of data centers seeking to connect to the ERCOT grid. Projects found in violation 'must be denied connection.' Developers must disclose tax incentives, power sourcing, water use and ownership. ERCOT reported more than 1,800 large-load requests totaling about 474 GW, which Abbott said are about 90% data centers. ERCOT paused its Batch Zero study, and the PUCT granted good-cause exceptions to an August 7 classification deadline. ERCOT says it will not finish the Batch Zero study by April 9, 2027, and is targeting a December 10 audit filing.
whyItMatters: This freezes the main path to grid power in the nation's fastest-growing large-load market. It will also likely reorder the Texas queue by weeding out speculative requests. BloombergNEF, as reported by Utility Dive, estimated the Texas pause threatens up to 20% of the U.S. development pipeline.
affected: About 300 Batch Zero large loads of 75 MW or more; 17 large loads (~6.6 GW) that passed stability studies but still need energization approval; ERCOT transmission planning; Texas utilities (Oncor, CenterPoint, AEP Texas).
watchNext: Responses to ERCOT's audit RFIs, with more rounds possible in October and November. ERCOT/PUCT audit report targeted for about December 10, 2026, ahead of the PUCT December open meeting. Watch for a revised Batch Zero timeline.

title: New York EO 62 pauses state DEC permits for data centers of 50 MW or more pending statewide GEIS
whatHappened: Executive Order 62, signed July 14, 2026, directs DEC to hold in abeyance all discretionary permit applications for new or expanded data centers that consume or can consume 50 MW or more. It covers applications not deemed complete before that date. Local government approvals are excluded. The hold lasts until the Department of Public Service completes a Generic Environmental Impact Statement under SEQRA; the order sets no deadline for it. The order also directs DPS to form a Data Center Interconnection Working Group and ESD to post a Community Investment Framework, each within 60 days. DEC must deliver a water-withdrawal report within 12 months.
whyItMatters: This is the first statewide permitting pause in the country, and other governors have since cited it. It freezes large new campuses in New York for an open-ended period and signals rate-class and 'bring your own power' requirements to follow.
affected: Proposed 50 MW+ campuses upstate and on Long Island; NYPA/NYISO large-load planning; crypto and AI developers; localities with their own moratoriums (e.g., Brookhaven).
watchNext: Interconnection Working Group and Community Investment Framework (due about mid-September 2026), the GEIS scoping and hearing schedule, and the pending Responsible Data Center Development Act (20 MW threshold) in the Legislature.

title: PJM 2028/29 capacity auction clears at $325/MW-day cap and falls 6,831 MW short of reliability requirement
whatHappened: PJM announced July 14, 2026 that its 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction cleared 138,318 MW at the $325.00/MW-day cap in all zones, the third straight auction at the ceiling. Procured capacity was 6,831 MW below the reliability requirement, which PJM called the first RTO-wide shortfall in its history. PJM said the forecast peak was about 2,000 MW higher than for the prior auction, driven by data center additions. Its simulation suggests an uncapped price of about $554.72/MW-day. Total auction cost was about $16.4 billion.
whyItMatters: A shortfall at the cap means PJM cannot buy enough capacity for projected data center growth. That fuels state pressure for 'bring your own generation' rules and backstop procurement, and keeps affordability central to the 2026 campaigns in PJM states.
affected: All PJM load-serving entities and ratepayers; Northern Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania and New Jersey data center developers; generators; PJM governors.
watchNext: The 2029/2030 BRA is scheduled for December 2026 under the same collar, and the reliability backstop procurement has been delayed.

title: FERC issues show cause orders to six RTOs on large-load interconnection rules
whatHappened: On June 18, 2026, FERC issued six Federal Power Act Section 206 show cause orders, one each to PJM (EL26-67), MISO, SPP (EL26-68), CAISO, NYISO and ISO-NE. The orders preliminarily find that their tariffs lack adequate rules for large loads, defined as peak demand above 50 MW interconnecting above 69 kV. Each RTO had 30 days to report on resource adequacy for large loads and 60 days to justify its tariff or file reforms. The five reform areas are study processes, preventing cost shifting, co-location and behind-the-meter generation, new services for flexible loads, and studying generation that serves nearby loads. The action responds to DOE Secretary Wright's October 23, 2025 Section 403 letter, and FERC said the RM26-4 rulemaking remains open.
whyItMatters: This is the main federal action on data center grid access. It moves toward standard interconnection rules and cost protections across most of the U.S. outside ERCOT and non-RTO utilities, without FERC asserting new jurisdiction over retail load interconnection.
affected: Data center developers in all six FERC-jurisdictional RTOs; transmission owners; state regulators; ratepayers. ERCOT and non-RTO utilities are not covered.
watchNext: FERC action on RTO responses. PJM filed August 13, 2026 proposing an Interim Resource Adequacy Service; MISO and its transmission owners committed to a full response by November 16, 2026. FERC may also issue orders for non-RTO utilities under RM26-4.

caveats: FERC.gov returned 403 on fetch, so details were confirmed through Utility Dive, Duane Morris and other summaries. Some secondary sources cite a 20 MW threshold, which was the ANOPR proposal; the show cause orders use 50 MW. title: FERC orders PJM to create co-location transmission services for data centers
whatHappened: On December 18, 2025, FERC found PJM's tariff unjust and unreasonable in Docket EL25-49-000 because it lacked clear rates, terms and conditions for generators serving co-located load. FERC directed PJM to offer three new transmission services as alternatives to Network Integration Transmission Service: interim non-firm, Firm Contract Demand and Non-Firm Contract Demand. It also directed PJM to revise its behind-the-meter generation rules with a transition for existing customers, and set a paper hearing on rates. Compliance filings were due January 20 and February 16, 2026, and paper-hearing replies were due April 17, 2026.
whyItMatters: This sets the first FERC framework for co-locating data centers at power plants in the largest U.S. market. It shapes nuclear and gas co-location deals and how much those loads pay for grid service.
affected: PJM data center developers pursuing co-location (e.g., at nuclear plants); generators such as Constellation and Talen; PJM ratepayers and transmission owners.
watchNext: FERC ruling on the paper hearing rates and on PJM's further compliance filings (ER26-1088).

title: FERC only partly approves PJM data center backstop procurement; PJM delays auction and DOE presses for cost protections
authority: FERC; PJM Interconnection; U.S. Department of Energy
whatHappened: On September 29, 2026, FERC only partly approved PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement for data center-driven needs (ER26-3380). Chair Laura Swett called it a 'deeply flawed, eleventh-hour procurement mechanism.' PJM postponed the auction, which had been set to accept offers September 30 to October 21, with no new timeline. On October 7, DOE filed a rare statement of position urging PJM to adopt FERC's revisions, allocate backstop costs using updated load forecasts, and ensure large loads fund their own generation under the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. PJM plans a revised filing by October 29 after an October 22 special Members Committee meeting.
whyItMatters: The backstop is PJM's main near-term tool for closing the capacity gap that data centers created. Delays and federal pressure over who pays will shape costs and timing for new large loads across 13 states and DC.
affected: PJM large-load applicants; generators offering into the backstop; PJM ratepayers and state consumer advocates.
watchNext: PJM special Members Committee on October 22, 2026, revised FERC filing by October 29, 2026, and the December 2026 BRA.

whatHappened: On September 21, 2026, Gov. Newsom signed AB 1577 (reporting), AB 2383 and SB 886 (CPUC data center rates covering grid connection and supply costs), SB 1168 (rate structures), AB 2469 (water-use disclosure before local approval), AB 2619 (water supply planning) and SB 887 (removing data centers from blanket CEQA streamlining). The Data Center Coalition opposed the bills, which passed largely along party lines.
whyItMatters: California is a constrained market (Silicon Valley, Santa Clara). Mandated data center rate classes and the end of CEQA shortcuts raise costs and timelines for new large loads in PG&E and SVP territory.
affected: Santa Clara/Silicon Valley Power, PG&E Rule 30 applicants, Imperial Valley proposals; CPUC; local land-use agencies.

title: Virginia EO 22 creates Data Center Accountability Framework; Spanberger seeks end to by-right approvals over 25 MW
whatHappened: On September 18, 2026, Gov. Spanberger signed Executive Order 22. It bans executive-branch agencies from entering into or requiring NDAs for data center projects, creates a planning and community engagement toolkit for localities, expedites noise regulations, orders a review of diesel and other backup generation, and creates an AI Task Force. According to Virginia Mercury, VEDP must stop site-readiness help through expedited programs for projects of 25 MW or more. For the 2027 General Assembly she proposed requiring local approval and ending by-right approval for data centers over 25 MW, removing future large data centers from fast-track permitting, allocating more transmission, generation and PJM interconnection costs to data centers, and limiting on-site gas generation.
whyItMatters: Virginia is the world's largest data center market. The order itself is modest, but the legislative package would rewrite land-use and cost rules there if a Democratic-controlled General Assembly enacts it in 2027.
affected: Loudoun, Prince William, Culpeper, Hampton Roads and Southside Virginia markets; Dominion and NOVEC; developers that rely on by-right zoning; diesel backup fleets.
watchNext: Bill drafting ahead of the January 2027 General Assembly session. HB 1515 (statewide moratorium) was carried over to 2027. Also watch SCC review of the NextEra-Dominion merger.

title: Healey order bars state permits for data centers over 25 MW without local approval and community benefits agreement
whatHappened: Gov. Healey signed an executive order on September 8, 2026 covering data centers with peak demand above 25 MW. State permits cannot advance unless the developer shows compliance with the state's Data Center Framework and has filed a community benefits agreement with the host community. Covered projects must procure clean electricity equal to their annual consumption or pay into a Ratepayer Protection Fund. MassDEP is to set up an alternative compliance payment mechanism by the end of 2026. The order bars non-disclosure agreements between state agencies and data centers. Healey said it does not apply to the Lowell project already underway.
whyItMatters: Massachusetts is a small market, but the order gives municipalities an effective veto and adds a clean-energy procurement mandate. That combination is becoming a template in Democratic-led states.
affected: Proposed 274 MW Westfield project; New England developers; municipalities negotiating CBAs; ISO-NE large-load planning.
watchNext: Municipal guidance from EEA and the Executive Office of Economic Development due by December 31, 2026, and MassDEP's alternative compliance payment design by year-end 2026.

title: Pennsylvania EO 2026-05 makes local approval a precondition for DEP data center permits and ties tax exemption to 'GRID' terms
whatHappened: On August 18, 2026, Gov. Shapiro signed EO 2026-05. Under it, DEP will not issue any permit for a covered data center until the project has all required local approvals. Developers who sign a binding Consent Order and Agreement committing to the Governor's GRID Requirements can get rolling DEP review. GRID covers paying the full cost of new energy infrastructure, community engagement, local hiring and CBAs, and water conservation. Non-signers cannot begin DEP review until local approvals are secured. Applicants not meeting GRID will not receive the Computer Data Center Equipment sales tax exemption, and NDAs for data center projects are barred. Law-firm summaries say the order covers projects above 25 MW and removes AI data centers from Fast Track permitting.
whyItMatters: Pennsylvania is a fast-growing PJM market. Conditioning the main sales-tax incentive and DEP permits on binding commitments raises the cost and time to develop there, especially for projects without local consent. Law firms expect legal challenges.
affected: PJM-region campuses in Pennsylvania (e.g., Homer City, Amazon Susquehanna-area projects, western PA gas-fired campuses); townships using curative-amendment pauses; DEP and Department of Revenue.
watchNext: Department of Revenue guideline updates for the exemption program, any litigation over the order, and SB 1345 (local 18-month moratorium authority) in the General Assembly.

title: New Jersey enacts Data Center Fair Share Act creating separate rate class for data centers of 50 MW or more
authority: Governor Mikie Sherrill; New Jersey Legislature
whatHappened: Gov. Sherrill signed the Data Center Fair Share Act (S731/A796) on July 7, 2026. It directs the BPU to set service standards for large data center customers at each electric utility, with a threshold no greater than 50 MW, cut from 100 MW in an earlier draft. It covers new and existing data centers and aggregates co-located or commonly owned facilities. Customers must post financial guarantees covering at least 85% of requested service for 10 years. Large data centers are curtailed before residential customers in emergencies, and projects that commit to their own clean generation or storage get interconnection priority. The BPU has 12 months to set standards, after which each utility has 180 days to file a tariff.
whyItMatters: This adds a top-tier PJM state to the large-load tariff group with some of the strictest collateral and curtailment terms so far. It raises the carrying cost of speculative New Jersey requests. Former Gov. Murphy had pocket-vetoed a similar bill earlier in 2026.
affected: Data centers in PSE&G, JCP&L, ACE and RECO territories; existing northern NJ colocation operators; BPU.
watchNext: BPU standards due by about July 2027, then utility tariff filings within 180 days. Also watch litigation over the 38+ municipal bans.

title: Pritzker halts new Illinois data center tax-incentive agreements from July 1
whatHappened: On June 5, 2026, Gov. Pritzker directed the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity to stop processing new Data Center Investment Program agreements starting July 1, 2026. Existing agreements are honored. The POWER Act (HB 5513) had missed the May 31 spring deadline, and Pritzker asked lawmakers to pass reforms on energy costs, water reporting and community agreements in the fall veto session. A state report found 27 data centers received more than $983 million in benefits from 2020 to 2024.
whyItMatters: Illinois (Chicago metro) is a top-five market. Pausing new incentive certificates changes the economics for new hyperscale entrants and links the incentives' return to a broader regulatory deal.
affected: Chicago-area and downstate campuses seeking new certificates; ComEd and Ameren Illinois large-load customers; building trades.
watchNext: The fall veto session (October–November 2026) on the POWER Act. The Illinois Policy Institute argues DCEO lacks authority to pause certificates, so a legal challenge is possible.

title: DOE emergency orders tap data center backup generators and keep fossil plants online
whatHappened: During 2026, DOE issued Federal Power Act Section 202(c) orders authorizing grid operators to direct data centers and other large loads to run their backup generation as a last resort. Recipients included ERCOT (Order 202-26-01, Jan. 24), PJM (202-26-06, Jan. 26) and Duke Energy (202-26-07, Jan. 26). On May 18, 2026, Order 202-26-23 let PJM deploy backup generation at data centers and other major facilities from May 18 to 20. DOE also repeatedly extended 90-day orders keeping retiring plants online, including J.H. Campbell (MI), Eddystone (PA), Schahfer and Culley (IN), Craig 1 (CO) and Centralia (WA), with the latest renewals running into November–December 2026.
whyItMatters: Federal emergency authority now treats data center backup fleets as a grid reliability resource. That raises questions about generator run-hours, air permits and cost allocation. The plant-retention orders keep fossil units online partly on load-growth grounds, and their costs are spread to ratepayers.
affected: Data center operators with diesel or gas backup fleets in PJM, ERCOT, Duke and SPP territories; RTOs; owners of retiring coal and gas plants; ratepayers bearing 202(c) costs.
watchNext: Winter 2026–27 202(c) orders, and renewals of plant-retention orders expiring Nov. 14 (Campbell), Nov. 20 (Eddystone) and Dec. 18 (Schahfer/Culley).

title: PJM Board issues large-load CIFP decision, directing backstop procurement and transitional measures
whatHappened: On January 16, 2026, the PJM Board issued its decisional letter concluding the Critical Issue Fast Path on large load additions. It directed a package of partly transitional measures, including development of a reliability backstop procurement with defined price, term and quantity, with staff to address cost allocation. A day earlier, on January 15, the White House and PJM-state governors signed a statement of principles urging PJM to change its tariff for large loads. PJM filed the Reliability Backstop Procurement at FERC on July 31, 2026 (ER26-3380).

affected: Large-load applicants across PJM; transmission owners; state regulators; generators bidding into backstop procurement.
watchNext: FERC action on PJM's revised backstop filing (due October 29, 2026) and the December 2026 BRA.

title: Virginia SCC creates GS-5 rate class for 25 MW+ customers with minimum-demand obligations
whatHappened: In its November 25, 2025 final order in Dominion Energy Virginia's 2025 biennial review (PUR-2025-00058), the SCC created a GS-5 rate class for customers demanding 25 MW or more, effective January 1, 2027. These customers must pay at least 85% of contracted distribution and transmission demand and 60% of generation demand. The SCC approved base-rate increases of $565.7 million for 2026 and $209.9 million for 2027, against Dominion's requested $822 million and $345 million, and set ROE at 9.8%.

watchNext: GS-5 takes effect January 1, 2027. Also watch Dominion's IRP update and SCC review of the NextEra-Dominion merger (evidentiary hearing scheduled November 17, 2026).

title: EO 14318 fast-tracks federal permitting for data centers, revokes Biden AI infrastructure order
whatHappened: On July 23, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14318, "Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure" (90 FR 35385). It defines Qualifying Projects as those with at least $500 million in committed capital expenditure, more than 100 MW of incremental load, national-security purposes, or designation by a cabinet secretary. It directs new NEPA categorical exclusions, FAST-41 dashboard coverage, EPA streamlining and Brownfield/Superfund site reuse, a programmatic ESA consultation, review of Clean Water Act nationwide permits, and federal land offerings by Interior, Energy and Defense. It revokes EO 14141 of January 14, 2025.
whyItMatters: This is the main federal framework for data center permitting and federal-land siting, and later DOE site awards and EPA rule changes build on it. It mostly affects projects with a federal nexus. It does not preempt state or local zoning, permitting or utility regulation.
affected: Hyperscale and AI campus developers with federal permits, funding or land; DOE, DOI and DOD site programs; EPA and Army Corps permitting staff.
watchNext: Track agency implementation: new NEPA categorical exclusions, Clean Water Act nationwide permit revisions, and further federal-land lease awards.

whatHappened: Senate Bill 6 (89th Legislature, Sen. title: Alabama PSC adopts review procedure for Alabama Power data center contracts, with 90-day auto-approval
whatHappened: According to Alabama Daily News, the Alabama PSC on October 6, 2026 unanimously adopted a procedure for evaluating Alabama Power contracts with large-load data centers of 150 MW or more on a single site. Contracts are automatically approved if the commission does not vote within 90 days. Alabama Power must file a public petition naming the entities, maximum capacity and location, and submit full contracts and cost-impact estimates confidentially to the PSC and Attorney General under SB 270's public-interest standard. No public hearing is required. Alabama Power has 10 days to file a conforming tariff.
whyItMatters: This gives a fast, predictable approval path in a Southeast market, while adding some transparency. Advocates say the auto-approval clause weakens accountability.

title: MISO files fast-track Large Load Addition Resource Study pairing 200 MW+ loads with new generation
authority: Midcontinent Independent System Operator (filing at FERC)
whatHappened: On October 2, 2026, MISO asked FERC to approve a Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS). It is a 120-day study for loads above 200 MW paired with new generation in the same local resource zone. Up to 10 applications would be studied in each of three annual windows, with generation and load in service within three years and paired for at least 15 years, and non-refundable deposits required. MISO requested a decision by December 2. The filing responds partly to FERC's June finding that MISO's large-load rules were inadequate.
whyItMatters: LARS would create a faster lane for 'bring your own generation' data centers in the central U.S., which could shift siting toward MISO states with available gas and land.
affected: Hyperscale projects in Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin; MISO utilities (Entergy, Ameren, Xcel, Consumers, DTE, NIPSCO).
watchNext: FERC decision requested by December 2, 2026. First study window planned for early 2027.

title: NC regulators deny Duke Energy Progress gas turbine, calling data center load forecasts insufficiently reliable
whatHappened: On September 18, 2026, the NCUC denied Duke Energy Progress' request to build a 255 MW hydrogen-capable simple-cycle gas turbine at its Smith Energy Complex in Richmond County, estimated at $584 million. The commission said much of the projected load growth 'appears to be based upon anticipated data center customer additions' and found it 'insufficiently reliable.' It also said Duke had not shown how it would meet its White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge commitments for the unit. Duke said it is reviewing next steps.

title: House passes Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3; Senate effort blocked
whatHappened: On September 16, 2026, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340, Reps. Gabe Evans and Kathy Castor) 417-3 under suspension, after a 52-0 Energy and Commerce markup on July 21. The bill amends PURPA section 111(d) to require state regulators to consider, within one year, standards making data center loads of 100 MW or more pay the full incremental cost of generation, transmission and distribution upgrades, with financial assurances and exit-cost protection. It does not mandate adoption. In the Senate, a unanimous consent request on September 17 drew an objection, and a September 30 vote failed 57-43, short of 60. Democrats called the bill "toothless" and pointed to Sen. Heinrich's GRID Savings Act and Sen. Van Hollen's bill instead.
whyItMatters: Near-unanimous House support shows bipartisan agreement on data center cost allocation. But the consider-only PURPA approach leaves the outcome to state commissions, and Senate passage before the midterms looks unlikely.
affected: State PUCs and non-regulated utilities; data center developers above 100 MW; ratepayers.
watchNext: Senate action after the November 2026 midterms (lame duck), and competing Democratic bills that would give FERC jurisdiction over loads of 150 MW or more.

title: EO 14421 declares national emergency over foreign bulk-power equipment, citing data center load
whatHappened: On August 26, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14421, declaring a national emergency over foreign-produced bulk-power system equipment. It authorizes DOE to prohibit, condition or unwind transactions involving covered foreign entities when it finds sabotage, cyber or supply risks, and to require monitoring or removal of installed equipment, for facilities of 69 kV and above. title: South Dakota enacts data center 'bill of rights' (SB 135), rejects moratorium

title: New Jersey requires semiannual data center water and energy reporting to BPU

whatHappened: On August 27, 2026, Gov. Sherrill signed S3379/A4096, requiring data center owners and operators to file semiannual reports with the BPU. whatHappened: On April 7, 2026, Port Washington voters approved a referendum requiring voter approval before the city creates any tax incremental financing district worth more than $10 million. whyItMatters: Voters directly constrained the local financing tool used for hyperscale deals. It is a model for ballot-box challenges to data center incentives.

title: EO 14365 targets state AI laws but carves data center infrastructure out of proposed preemption
whatHappened: On December 11, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14365, "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence." It creates a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws, orders Commerce to identify "onerous" state AI laws within 90 days, and conditions some BEAD non-deployment funds on states not having such laws. Its legislative recommendation for a preemptive federal framework would not preempt state laws on AI compute and data center infrastructure, other than generally applicable permitting reforms.
whyItMatters: The carve-out means the administration's preemption push is not aimed at state or local data center siting, tax or utility rules. Those levers stay with states, while state AI model regulation faces federal pressure.
affected: State legislatures weighing AI and data center bills; AI developers; BEAD grant recipients.
watchNext: Whether Congress takes up a federal AI framework that keeps the data center infrastructure exclusion, and any DOJ task force suits against state laws.
